profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the academic lead of an international virtual exchange initiative and a university learning design manager at a partner institution who are preparing a cross-institution pilot based on the International Online Collaboration Competencies (IOCC) framework. The context is that three courses in different countries will pilot shared learning tasks next semester, and the two workstreams now need to align on what materials will be handed off to instructors, which wording/version of the competency framework will be embedded in templates, and what counts as completed preparation before the faculty onboarding webinar. The agenda is to review progress on the competency framework materials, confirm the faculty package, align the course-outcome mapping handoff, and set deadlines for uploading materials into the shared teaching environment. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on who will deliver the framework documents, what will be circulated to instructors next week, and when the pilot setup will be considered ready.

members.name: Dr. Lena Hofmann
members.role: Academic Lead for Virtual Exchange Curriculum
members.expertise: Internationalization of the curriculum, intercultural collaboration pedagogy, faculty development
members.background: Associate professor who co-authored the local adaptation of the IOCC consensus study and oversees the academic coherence of a multi-university pilot involving business, engineering, and education courses.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to preserve fidelity to the published IOCC framework while minimizing last-minute debates with faculty, and she is worried that over-operationalizing the competencies too early will make academics push back on the model.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'framework,' they mean the published six-domain structure and 34 competencies as represented in the manuscript appendix, not later implementation simplifications.
A 'pilot-ready rubric' is ready once the competency language is stable enough for faculty review, even if platform formatting and scoring mechanics are still unfinished.
The 'faculty package' is primarily an instructor-oriented briefing set, so student-facing tools and facilitation notes are optional follow-on materials rather than part of the core handoff.
If the courses are 'mapped,' that means each course has been connected at the planning level to relevant IOCC domains; full criterion-level tagging can happen during implementation.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.role: Learning Design and Assessment Operations Manager
members.expertise: Curriculum implementation, LMS workflows, assessment rubrics, multi-course deployment
members.background: Former instructional designer who now manages template rollout, reporting fields, and faculty support processes for cross-campus digital learning initiatives.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid ambiguous materials that generate support tickets during launch, and he is concerned that if definitions and artifacts are not operationalized now, his team will have to rebuild everything under time pressure.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'framework,' they mean the implementation artifact that instructors and systems will actually use, even if wording has been lightly normalized from the publication.
A 'pilot-ready rubric' is something instructors can directly use in the LMS with scoring rows, labels, and no unresolved interpretation gaps.

The standard 'faculty package' for a rollout includes all companion materials instructors need to run the activity without follow-up requests, including student self-check tools and facilitation guidance.
If a course is 'mapped,' every assessable element that will appear in reporting needs explicit competency tags in the curriculum system, not just a conceptual alignment document.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a pilot-ready rubric
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the IOCC rubric as 'pilot-ready.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the competency set and descriptors are academically stable enough to circulate to faculty for the pilot, even if scoring levels and LMS formatting are finalized later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the rubric is operationally deployable in the LMS with scoring rows, labels, and no additional interpretation work required from instructors.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both regularly use 'pilot-ready' as a positive status label, and in a coordination meeting it sounds like a routine progress update rather than a term that needs unpacking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use the 'Round 3 wording' for the competencies.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the wording in the final consensus-study appendix attached to the accepted manuscript.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to an internal post-acceptance spreadsheet that preserved the same structure but lightly edited phrasing for readability and consistency in templates.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both documents are treated locally as the latest authoritative phrasing, both stem from the same study, and the wording differences are subtle enough that the phrase 'Round 3 wording' feels unambiguous.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the faculty package
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss sending out the 'faculty package' before the onboarding webinar.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the package includes the framework overview, competency list, and sample learning task examples for instructors.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the package also includes student-facing self-assessment sheets, facilitation notes, and the implementation checklist because those are standard support materials in rollout packs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'faculty package' sounds like an established bundle, and each person defaults to the conventions of their own workstream without realizing the boundary differs.

misalignment_points.topic: When course mapping is considered done
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the course-to-competency 'mapping' should be done before the webinar.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means each pilot course should have its intended learning outcomes linked to relevant IOCC domains in the planning sheet so faculty can see conceptual fit.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means each rubric criterion and tracked activity in the curriculum system should be tagged down to the relevant competencies so reports can be generated after the pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely aiming for completion before faculty onboarding, but 'mapping' is a familiar umbrella term that hides different thresholds for what completed work entails.

The main thing today is to confirm that next week's instructor-facing set goes out cleanly and still reflects the consensus framework rather than drifting into implementation shortcuts.

So I want to hear that the rubric and faculty package are pilot-ready before the webinar.
